items.title: Recent advances in AI are creating a 'paradigm shift' for robotics - Berkeley News
items.summary: Traditionally, engineers can directly program the software that tells robots how to perceive objects, plan movements and control their actions, a process called model-based robotics. Or, with model-free robotics, they can train robots to learn behaviors from demonstrations through imitation learning. The first approach requires extensive engineering, while the second needs enormous amounts of data and time. [...] “Robots are advancing quickly, but developing them for real-world environments remains slow, data-intensive and difficult to scale,” Huang said. “Working with UC Berkeley, NVIDIA is helping advance a new approach combining agentic AI, simulation and open industrial task-focused benchmarks to help developers rapidly test and improve robot behavior before deployment.” [...] Earlier this year, he and his team began experimenting with a change to the way the robot code is organized. Using a framework they called Graph-as-Policy, robot tasks are segmented into individual skills, such as finding an object, planning a grasp and moving the gripper without collisions. Goldberg likened it to individual building blocks that fit together into something much larger.

items.title: Top Robotics Stocks With Strong Potential for Long-Term Growth
items.summary: With orders accelerating, humanoid pilots becoming contracts, surgical robotics gaining regulatory clarity and defense autonomy topping budget priorities, U.S. robotics enters 2027 with diversified demand drivers, positioning sector leaders well as adoption scales across factories, hospitals and homes. [...] U.S. robotics stocks enter the final stretch of 2026 on firmer footing, as September through early November brought a wave of commercial deployments, regulatory progress and government funding signals. North American robot orders hit their strongest quarter of the year, humanoids moved from demos toward contracted factory work, the FDA outlined a clearer path for surgical robots, and the Pentagon made autonomy a top budget priority. Together, these developments point to a broadening demand base [...] U.S. robotics demand strengthened through the fall. The Association for Advancing Automation reported that North American companies ordered 10,989 robots worth $723.5 million in the third quarter of 2026, up 24.8% year over year, with semiconductor and electronics orders nearly doubling. Humanoids moved closer to factory floors as Boston Dynamics opened its Robotics Metaplant Application Center in Georgia on Sept. 21 to train Atlas for Hyundai, which plans to deploy 25,000 units globally.

items.title: Inside App State’s Robotics Lab: Students explore the future of human–robot collaboration | Appalachian Today
items.summary:
Students work with a variety of robotic platforms, including robotic arms that handle objects, humanoid robots such as Pepper and NAO that are designed to interact with people and mobile robots that can move through an environment while manipulating objects. These platforms help students explore how robot behavior, movement and communication influence interactions with people. [...] Current lab projects focus on helping robots better understand and respond to the people around them. Researchers are investigating how robots can adapt their behavior over time, work safely alongside people and use different types of information to make more informed decisions.

One research area examines how robots can adjust their actions as people move nearby, an important challenge in workplaces where humans and robots share the same space. [...] This brief video offers a behind-the-scenes look at the Yeganeh Robotics (YeRo) Lab in App State’s College of Arts and Sciences. Demonstrations include a Go2 quadruped robot, often called a “robot dog,” navigating its surroundings while maintaining balance, and a robotic arm transferring an object between locations on a workbench. These examples illustrate the types of robotic systems and research questions student researchers are exploring in the lab.

items.title: MTSU Hosts Interstate Hackathon to Expand Quantum Computing Education
items.summary: As quantum computing advances from laboratory research toward emerging applications, preparing people to turn this technology into practical solutions is becoming increasingly important. [...] “Quantum computing is advancing rapidly, but developing the technology is only part of the equation,” said Hanna Terletska, professor of physics and director of MTSU’s QRISE Center. “We also need people who know how to use it to solve meaningful problems. Through this hackathon, we are giving students the opportunity to move beyond theory, gain hands-on experience and begin thinking about how quantum computing could address real challenges in science and industry.” [...] To prepare participants, organizers provided four weeks of introductory training in quantum computing fundamentals, IBM’s Qiskit programming tools, quantum algorithms and potential scientific and industrial applications. During the three-day competition, students worked in interdisciplinary teams on molecular simulation, quantum machine learning and optimization challenges. items.title: What will it take to integrate quantum computing into drug discovery? | Drug Discovery News
items.summary:
Quantum computing is often discussed alongside AI as another technology that could accelerate drug discovery. But while AI uses patterns in data to generate predictions and hypotheses, quantum computing takes a fundamentally different approach to processing information. [...] While classical computing relies on conventional bits, which represent information as either a zero or a one, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, which can exist in multiple states at once. This makes them potentially well suited to simulating the behavior of electrons and their interactions – processes that underpin chemical reactions and molecular properties but can be challenging to capture using classical computational methods.

It's a completely new computing modality. [...] Quantum computing has the potential to accelerate and enhance drug discovery. But even as researchers work to improve the hardware and software, significant gaps remain in the infrastructure needed to bring the technology into biotechnology. Access to quantum computing remains difficult and expensive, while expertise spanning both quantum computing and biology is still limited.

We need people who understand each field and people who can work across both.

items.title: Chicago’s bid to lead the country in quantum computing | IBM Quantum Computing Blog
items.summary: The team at UChicago and IBM swapped in sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), a powerful quantum-centric supercomputing approach for solving chemistry problems, as the fragment solver. The resulting method, LASSQD, resembles LASSCF in important ways. It picks fragments, sends a circuit for each one to IBM quantum hardware, recombines the results, updates the orbitals classically, and repeats until the answer converges. [...] The region is also home to important quantum computing research. In 2026, a joint team from the University of Chicago and IBM demonstrated quantum advantage on a structured computational task, offering an alternative to traditional random circuit sampling benchmarks. Running on an IBM quantum system, the experiment leveraged 70 logical qubits to complete a calculation in approximately 15 minutes, surpassing the practical capabilities of today's leading classical simulation methods while [...] Following the announcement of the expanded collaboration in April 2026, the joint team delivered its first demonstration within six months: a computation of Cu₃C₆O₆, a strongly correlated kagome-lattice metal, using the integrated DeltaAI and IBM Quantum systems. The results will be presented at SC26 in November, highlighting the pace of innovation enabled by this collaboration.
